For 2026, here's where the 401(k) limits landed:
- Employee deferral: $24,500
- Catch-up if you're 50 or older: $8,000
- If you're between 60 and 63, the enhanced catch-up is $11,250 instead
These apply to your total deferrals across all employer plans.
Great question! The 401(k) contribution limit this year is $23,500, and if you're over 50 you can add a $7,500 catch-up on top of that.
You can put up to $7,500 into IRAs for 2026 - that's combined across traditional and Roth, not per account. Since you mentioned you turn 52 this year, you also get an extra $1,100 catch-up.
Sure! For tax year 2026 the IRA contribution limit is $6,500. You can split that between a Roth and a traditional IRA however you like.

Looking at your account, your current 401(k) balance is $12,340.18. With your $85,000 salary, bumping your contribution from 4% to 6% would mean about $5,100 a year going in, and your employer match of 3% adds another $2,550. Want me to update your election?
For 2026, the HSA contribution limit for self-only coverage is $4,300 and the family limit is $8,750. Remember that employer contributions count toward these caps.

HSA limits at a glance:
* 2026: self-only $4.4k, family $8.75k
* 2027 (already announced): $4,500 self-only and $9,000 family
If you're 55+, you can add a $1,000 catch-up either year.

If you have family coverage under a high-deductible plan, you can contribute up to $8,300 to your HSA for 2026. Your current payroll deduction of $250 per paycheck puts you at $6,500 for the year, so you have some room left.
Social Security tax only applies to wages up to a cap, called the taxable maximum. For 2026 that cap is $176,100, so any earnings above that aren't subject to the Social Security portion of FICA.

The 2026 Social Security taxable maximum is 184,500 dollars. Since your salary is $210,000, you'll stop seeing Social Security withholding on your paychecks sometime in the fall once your year-to-date wages cross that line. Medicare tax keeps going regardless.

Beneficiaries received a 2.8% cost-of-living adjustment starting in January 2026, and SSA has announced a 3.6% COLA for 2027. On your current benefit of $2,140 a month, the 2027 increase would add roughly $77.
The Social Security COLA for 2026 was 3.2%, which is a bit higher than the year before. It's applied automatically - you don't need to do anything.

Since you're claiming before your full retirement age, the earnings test applies. If you're under FRA this year, you can earn up to $23,400 before SSA starts withholding $1 for every $2 above the limit. Your projected $31,000 from consulting would put you over.

Earnings test limits for people under full retirement age: $24,480 for 2026, rising to $25,560 in 2027. Above that, some benefits get withheld temporarily, but they're credited back once you reach FRA.
Short answer: you have to start taking required minimum distributions at age 72. Your first one can be delayed until April 1 of the following year, but then you'd take two in one year.

RMDs begin at 73 under current rules. If you miss one, the excise tax is 25% of the amount you should have withdrawn, reduced to 10% if you correct it within two years. Given your IRA balance of about $640,000, it's worth setting up automatic distributions.
Be careful here - missing a required minimum distribution triggers a 50% penalty on the amount you failed to take out. That's one of the steepest penalties in the tax code.

If you withdraw the $40,000 from your 401(k) now, it'll be taxed as ordinary income plus a 10% additional tax for early distribution, unless an exception applies. Another option: if the check is made out to you, you can still roll it into an IRA within 60 days and avoid both.
Good news - you have 90 days to complete an indirect rollover, so there's plenty of time to deposit that $18,250 check into your new IRA.

2026 standard deduction amounts:
- Single: $16,100
- Married filing jointly: $32,200
- Head of household: $24,150
If your itemized deductions (mortgage interest, state taxes, charity) don't exceed these, take the standard deduction.

For 2026 the standard deduction is $15,000 if you file single and $32,200 for married couples filing jointly. With your $9,400 in mortgage interest and $3,000 in donations, you're better off with the standard deduction.

You can give up to $19,000 per recipient in 2026 without filing a gift tax return. Since you're planning to give your daughter $25,000, you'd file Form 709 for the excess - but you almost certainly won't owe any tax; it just counts against your lifetime exemption.
The annual gift tax exclusion is $18,000 per recipient in 2026, and you and your spouse can each give that amount, so you could gift your son $36,000 together.
SIMPLE IRA limit for 2026 is $16,500. Your employer will also make either a matching or nonelective contribution on top of that.
Yes, SIMPLE plans have a lower cap than 401(k)s - it's $17k for 2026.

Let's map out your 2026 tax-advantaged savings. On a $140,000 salary you have three main buckets. First, your 401(k): the employee deferral limit is $24,500, and you're currently on pace for about $16,800, so you could increase your rate. Second, an IRA: you can contribute up to $7,500, though at your income a direct Roth contribution may be phased out, so look into a backdoor Roth. Third, because you have family HDHP coverage, your HSA limit is $8,750. Maxing all three would shelter a little over $40,000 this year.
In 2026 you can defer $24,500 into your 403(b). On top of that, your IRA limit is $7,000 - so between the two you can save quite a bit before touching a taxable brokerage account.
TSP participants aged 60-63 get a special super catch-up. For 2026 that's $10,000 on top of the regular limit, which is a nice boost if you're behind on savings.
Government 457(b) plans have their own separate limit, which is great because you can max it alongside a 403(b). The 457(b) deferral limit for 2026 is 23,500 dollars.

Whether Roth or traditional makes more sense really depends on whether you expect your tax rate to be higher now or in retirement. If you're early in your career and expect your income to grow, Roth contributions are often attractive. If you're in your peak earning years, the upfront deduction from traditional contributions can be more valuable. Many people split contributions between both to hedge.

Your HSA balance is $3,212.44 as of today. You've contributed $150 per paycheck this year, for a total of $3,150 so far, and your employer added $500 in January. You have one pending reimbursement for $86.20.

Here's a simple budget based on what you shared: take-home pay of $6,200 a month, rent $1,800, car payment $420, groceries around $650. That leaves roughly $3,330 for everything else. I'd suggest routing $1,000 of that to savings automatically before you see it.

Required minimum distributions are calculated by dividing your prior year-end account balance by a life expectancy factor from the IRS Uniform Lifetime Table. Your plan administrator or IRA custodian can usually calculate it for you, and many will set up automatic withdrawals.
For 2026 the regular 401(k) limit is $24,500, and the catch-up for 50+ is $7,500 in 2026, so your total could be $32,000 if you're 50 or older.
The Social Security wage base was $184,500 for 2026 and is going up to $192,300 in 2027. If you earn above that, your Social Security tax for the year is capped.
You'll be eligible for a self-only HSA contribution of $4,400 this year, and because you're 57, you can also make a catch-up contribution of $1,500 extra.
Since you're 53, you get an IRA catch-up. That's $1,000 for IRAs this year, on top of the base limit.
If you start Social Security early while still working, the earnings limit for 2026 is $26,000. Anything above that, SSA withholds $1 of benefits for every $2 you earn.
The HSA family limit for 2026 is $8,550. Since you switched to family coverage in March, your limit may be prorated unless you use the last-month rule.
Yep - for 2026 it's $24.5k for the 401(k) and $7.5k for an IRA. You can do both.
